gaps: No packaging/deployment contract at all — the reference treats a docker-compose.yml with a service named `server` on port 8000 and `GET /healthz` as normative (harness-critical); the candidate document is silent on packaging, deployment, or how an external harness/grader would build and reach the implementation.

The candidate never states the 'total chips in play are conserved hand-to-hand' invariant as an explicit design assertion the way the reference calls it out (it is only demonstrable by manually summing the worked example, not asserted as a property the design guarantees).

Minimum-bet-size legality (reference: 'BET only legal if amount >= big_blind') is not stated as its own rule for the candidate's BET case in §2.4 — it is only recoverable by noticing that §2.5's raise-amount formula (amount >= currentBet + minRaiseSize) happens to reduce to amount >= bigBlind when currentBet == 0, since BET/RAISE share one wire action. This is consistent but requires the reader to derive it rather than being stated directly, unlike the reference's explicit 'amount >= big_blind'.

No independent-oracle-style acceptance criteria or explicit note of how showdown payouts would be externally verified — the reference states this is what the harness checks; the candidate's document doesn't anticipate any such validation surface (arguably out of scope for a WebSocket-only design, but it is a concern the reference explicitly surfaces and the candidate doesn't).
superior_choices: The action-validation pipeline (§2.3) is a strictly ordered, seven-step precondition list run against a single serially-processed per-table engine — this is more mechanically precise and easier for two independent implementers to match exactly than the reference's prose description of the same invariant.

Explicit identity binding (§2.2): the server resolves seat from `connectionId → playerId → seatNo` and never trusts a client-supplied seat number. The reference states the current_actor-only invariant but never specifies how a request is bound to a seat/identity in the first place — this is a real hardening gap in the reference that the candidate closes.

Action idempotency via client-generated `actionId` (§2.7) handles retried/duplicate submissions safely (flaky connections re-sending after a timed-out ack) — the reference has no equivalent, and duplicate-submission handling is a real correctness concern for any live network protocol.

Server-driven turn timeout with a well-defined default action (CHECK if legal else FOLD) plus auto-sit-out after 3 consecutive timeouts (§2.8) — the reference doesn't address disconnected/idle players at all, leaving an unspecified stall condition that a later implementer would have to invent unilaterally.

Reconnection and STATE_SYNC (§2.9) plus `handSeq`/`actionSeq` gap detection (§6.3) give clients a well-defined way to recover a consistent view after a dropped connection — entirely absent from the reference, which only concerns itself with the synchronous request/response API.

The worked numeric example for side-pot construction (§5.2, A/B/C/D with 100/60/200/200) is concrete and independently checkable (560 = 100+60+200+200), which is pedagogically stronger than the reference's abstract algorithm alone and reduces the chance of two implementers diverging on the layering logic.

The message contract (§6) is fully concrete — every event's fields, recipients, and privacy markers are tabulated — versus the reference's API section, which explicitly defers the wire contract to an external HARNESS-CONTRACT.md and states only the packaging/port requirements inline.
summary: The candidate is an exceptionally rigorous, self-contained server design that matches or exceeds the reference on every core game-logic concern the brief calls out: turn enforcement is specified as a strict, ordered, race-free validation pipeline with explicit connection-to-seat identity binding (a hardening step the reference doesn't even address); the short all-in raise / full-raise-reopens-action distinction is handled with the same precision as the reference, including the heads-up dealer/blind exception and the all-players-all-in runout case; and the side-pot construction algorithm is not only equivalent to the reference's but illustrated with a fully worked, chip-conserving numeric example. The candidate goes further than the reference into production-grade concerns entirely absent there — action idempotency, server-driven turn timeouts with auto-sit-out, and reconnection/gap-detection via sequence numbers — none of which the reference's turn-state-machine description needs to consider because it is scoped purely to a REST API a harness drives directly. The one substantive gap is that the candidate never addresses packaging/deployment (no docker-compose, service name, port, or /healthz equivalent), which the reference treats as a normative, harness-critical section; the candidate also leaves the total-chips-conserved invariant and the BET minimum-amount rule implicit rather than stated outright, though both are recoverable from the rest of the document without contradiction. No internal contradictions or unresolved ambiguities were found — every decision that would otherwise need to be resolved unilaterally by an implementer (button rotation, blind posting order, minimum-raise bookkeeping, odd-chip distribution, reveal order) is pinned down explicitly.
